title: “Crea 2.6, pls eval ?HD”
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; local protocol and the attending nephrologist’s judgment come first.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident rotating on the renal consult service of a tertiary hospital in Pampanga. At 16:10 on Monday, a referral arrives through the hospital messaging system from the surgery service: “Bed 9, 68F, crea 2.6, pls eval ?HD. Tnx.” The “?HD” asks whether she needs hemodialysis.

The chart shows Mrs. Erlinda Castillo, 68, a retired public school teacher with type 2 diabetes and hypertension. She was admitted two days ago with an infected diabetic foot, had a computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the leg with contrast on admission, and underwent debridement under spinal anesthesia yesterday. She is on an intravenous antibiotic and ketorolac, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), for pain. Her creatinine was 1.8 mg/dL on admission and is 2.6 mg/dL today; potassium is 5.4 mmol/L. Your renal fellow, Dr. Paolo Lacson, is in the outpatient clinic and reachable by phone.

n1.prompt: The referral is one line. What do you do first?

choices.text: Open the chart and spend the next hour building a complete history and creatinine timeline, then go to the bedside.
choices.feedback: The timeline matters, but it answers no question yet, and nobody has checked whether anything is dangerous today. The question and the patient’s stability come first; the timeline comes after.
choices.then: At 17:00 you call the surgical resident and go to the bedside.

choices.text: Call the referring surgical resident to learn the real question, then go to the bedside and check potassium, fluid, acid, uremia, obstruction and circulation before taking the history.
choices.feedback: “Creatinine high” is not a question; determining the question is the first of Goldman’s ten consultation principles. Stability comes next, because potassium, fluid, acid, uremia and obstruction can kill or injure within hours, and none of them waits for the timeline.

choices.text: Reply in the chat: “Crea 2.6 is not dialysis level, no need for HD, will see tomorrow.”
choices.feedback: A creatinine value alone cannot answer whether a patient is safe tonight. The potassium trend, the urine output, the fluid status and the bladder are unknown, and you have answered a consultation without seeing the patient.
choices.then: Dr. Lacson reads the thread and asks you to see her now. You call the surgical resident and go to the bedside.

choices.text: Order a kidney ultrasound, a urinalysis and a full serology panel through the chat, and see her once the results return.
choices.feedback: Tests ordered before you know the question or the patient’s stability may miss the emergency. A broad serology panel rarely changes tonight’s decision, costs the family money, and delays the tests that matter.
choices.then: You cancel the serologies, call the surgical resident and go to the bedside.

n2.scene: The surgical resident says the team wants to know two things: does she need dialysis, and how should they dose her antibiotic? At the bedside Mrs. Castillo is awake, with a temperature of 38.2 °C and clear lungs. The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows no peaked T waves. She has passed no urine since 06:00 and complains of lower abdominal discomfort. The nurse’s bladder scan shows 720 mL.

choices.text: A fluid bolus, because her urine output is low.
choices.feedback: A full bladder is not a volume problem. Fluid given to a patient who cannot pass urine adds to the load without fixing anything.
choices.then: You withdraw the bolus suggestion and ask for a catheter. It drains 750 mL.

choices.text: A kidney ultrasound in the morning to look for hydronephrosis.
choices.feedback: The right idea, too slowly. The bladder scan already shows outlet obstruction, which is quick to fix and easy to miss; relieve it now and image later.
choices.then: You ask for a catheter now. It drains 750 mL.

choices.text: Intravenous furosemide to get the urine flowing.
choices.feedback: A diuretic cannot empty an obstructed bladder; it only adds urine behind the blockage. Until the outflow is open, the urine output tells you nothing about the kidneys.
choices.then: You cancel the order and ask for a catheter. It drains 750 mL.

choices.text: Relieve the obstruction now with a bladder catheter per the ward protocol, then chart urine output every hour.
choices.feedback: Obstruction is the cause of kidney injury that is quickest to fix and easiest to miss. Draining the bladder treats it and turns the urine output back into a measure of kidney function.

n3.scene: Her son, Mr. Jerome Castillo, shows you photos of laboratory slips on his phone: creatinine 1.5 mg/dL ten months ago and 1.6 mg/dL five months ago, from a diagnostic center in Angeles City. An older slip, three years ago, reads 0.9 mg/dL. Today’s 2.6 mg/dL came 48 hours after the admission value of 1.8 mg/dL.
n3.prompt: Which baseline do you write in the note?

choices.text: 1.6 mg/dL, the most recent outpatient value.
choices.feedback: Close. In Siew’s study the mean of outpatient values from 7 to 365 days before admission agreed best with nephrologists, better than the most recent value; here the difference is small, but the habit matters.
choices.then: You write the mean of the two values from the past year.

choices.text: 0.9 mg/dL, the lowest value she has ever had.
choices.feedback: The lowest value, especially an old one, makes the injury look larger than it is. Siew found that adding older values did not improve agreement with the nephrologists’ reference.
choices.then: You write the mean of the two values from the past year.

choices.text: About 1.55 mg/dL, the mean of the two outpatient values from the past year.
choices.feedback: The mean of last year’s stable outpatient values agreed best with nephrologists (intraclass correlation 0.91). Separately, the rise of 0.8 mg/dL in 48 hours already meets the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2012 definition of acute kidney injury (AKI), on top of a reduced baseline.

choices.text: No baseline in our chart, so record chronic kidney disease (CKD) based on today’s value.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2024 says chronicity needs at least three months of evidence and should not be assumed from one abnormal value. Her old slips may support CKD, but today’s rise is acute and must be named as such.
choices.then: You write the mean of the two values from the past year and record the acute rise.

n4.scene: A co-resident glances at the chart: “Contrast CT on admission, creatinine up two days later. Contrast nephropathy. Done.” The medication sheet shows ketorolac every eight hours since admission, and Mr. Castillo mentions herbal capsules “for sugar” that his mother buys online.
n4.prompt: How do you frame the problem and the work-up?

choices.text: Write one sentence with the tempo, syndrome and context; sort causes by perfusion, tubule, interstitium, glomerulus and obstruction; stop the ketorolac and the capsules; and order urinalysis with sediment and a kidney ultrasound.
choices.feedback: A sharp problem representation narrows the search, and asking “what else, and what would prove me wrong?” guards against premature closure. Sepsis, the NSAID, contrast, the herbal product and the obstruction each need a deliberate check, and each test ordered should change the next decision.

vitals.order: Ketorolac and capsules stopped; urinalysis, sediment, ultrasound

choices.text: Accept contrast nephropathy and leave the ketorolac running, since her pain control matters after debridement.
choices.feedback: This is premature closure, the most common cognitive error in Graber’s series. The NSAID blocks afferent vasodilation in a septic patient and may be part of the cause; leaving it running keeps harming the kidney.
choices.then: Dr. Lacson asks what else could explain the picture. You stop the ketorolac and the capsules and rewrite the plan.

vitals.order: Ketorolac and capsules stopped; urinalysis, sediment, ultrasound

choices.text: Send every serology available tonight so nothing is missed.
choices.feedback: Blanket testing is not a differential. It costs the family money and rarely changes tonight’s decision, while the urinalysis and sediment that would change it wait.
choices.then: You cancel most of the panel, stop the ketorolac and the capsules, and order the focused tests.

vitals.order: Ketorolac and capsules stopped; urinalysis, sediment, ultrasound

choices.text: Agree that contrast is the likely cause, but stop the ketorolac to be safe.
choices.feedback: The right action for an incomplete reason. You have still closed on one cause; the herbal product, the sepsis and the obstruction need a place in the differential, and the urine sediment can separate them.
choices.then: You also stop the capsules, write a full differential, and order urinalysis with sediment and a kidney ultrasound.

vitals.order: Ketorolac and capsules stopped; urinalysis, sediment, ultrasound

n5.scene: Your problem representation reads: “A 68-year-old woman with diabetes, a reduced baseline and sepsis from a foot infection has AKI over two days, from about 1.55 to 2.6 mg/dL, with urinary retention, after contrast, ketorolac and an unidentified herbal product.” Dr. Lacson agrees by phone. Her potassium on repeat is 5.3 mmol/L, and her urine is now flowing at 60 mL an hour. The surgical team changes shift at 19:00.
n5.prompt: How do you deliver the consultation?

choices.text: A complete note with the history first and the recommendations at the end of the second page; the night team will read it.
choices.feedback: A correct plan that is not found in time is a failed consultation. The referring team should see the answer in the first lines, and a time-sensitive plan needs a direct conversation.
choices.then: You move the answer to the top and call the surgical resident.

vitals.order: Note, call with read-back, owner named

choices.text: Lead the note with the answer (AKI, not dialysis tonight; antibiotic dosed for kidney function with pharmacy), numbered recommendations and if-then triggers; call the surgical resident for a read-back; have the fellow inform the attending; name the renal fellow at morning rounds as the owner.
choices.feedback: Goldman’s principles ask for a specific answer, contingency plans, direct communication and follow-up. I-PASS handoffs with a read-back by the receiver were associated with fewer medical errors in a before-and-after study, and AKI needs an owner beyond tonight.

vitals.order: Note, call with read-back, owner named

choices.text: A note with numbered recommendations, and a chat message to the ward: “See my note.”
choices.feedback: The note is good, but a chat message without acknowledgment does not confirm that anyone read it. Call, read back the triggers, and name who follows up.
choices.then: You call the surgical resident, read back the plan, and add the owner to the note.

vitals.order: Note, call with read-back, owner named

choices.text: Tell the surgical resident she is “cleared from the renal side” and that renal will sign off.
choices.feedback: AKI is not a one-night problem. In AKI-EPI, nearly half of intensive care patients with AKI left hospital with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², so someone must own the follow-up; signing off leaves no one.
choices.then: Dr. Lacson asks you to stay on the case. You write the triggers, call the surgical resident, and name the owner.

vitals.order: Note, call with read-back, owner named

end.title: Two days later
end.text: Mrs. Castillo’s creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL and falling, her urine flows, and her antibiotic is dosed for her kidney function. The ketorolac and the capsules stay stopped; the son has photographed the capsule label for the chart. The discharge plan names a creatinine check at a laboratory near her home in Mabalacat and a renal clinic visit, because AKI on a reduced baseline needs someone to follow it.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Get the real question first, then check potassium, fluid, acid, uremia, obstruction and circulation before the history.
  • Look at the bladder. Obstruction is quick to fix and easy to miss, and a diuretic or a bolus will not fix it.
  • Choose the baseline deliberately: the mean of last year’s stable outpatient values; do not assume chronicity from one result.
  • Say the problem in one sentence, then ask what else it could be and order only tests that change the next decision.
  • Lead with the answer, give if-then triggers, call for a read-back, and name the owner.

See Question and stability, The timeline, Problem representation and Note, call, handoff.
